posts.title: Fine-tuning Llama 2 for Mental Health Support: 240 Curated Responses Across 30 Categories
posts.subtitle: How we built an actually-helpful crisis-triage chatbot by curating by category, not by length.
posts.content:
# Fine-tuning Llama 2 for Mental Health Support

Most mental-health chatbots fail the same way: they give **long**, **empathetic-sounding**, but **useless** answers. We learned this in week one of building **MindMate**, when naive prompt-engineering produced paragraphs that read warm and recommended the user "reach out to a professional" — every single time.

That isn't a chatbot. That's a legal disclaimer.

## What we actually needed

We needed responses that did three things in under 80 words:

1. **Validate** what the user just said. Not paraphrase it — *acknowledge* it.
2. **Offer one concrete next step**. A breathing pattern, a grounding exercise, a single reframing — one.
3. **Escalate fast** if the user was in crisis. Real triage, not a polite nudge.

## Curating by category, not by length

We organised 240+ curated responses across 30+ mental-health categories — anxiety, panic, grief, sleep, identity, loneliness, work stress, relationship conflict, and so on. The unit of work was *category*, not *single response*.

This forced three discipline checks:

- **Within a category**: are we giving the same advice with different wording, or genuinely varying the tactic? (Answers within a category must rotate.) 
- **Across categories**: does the model accidentally recommend isolation for someone anxious, instead of connection? (Cross-category consistency.)
- **At the boundary**: when the user starts in anxiety and reveals suicidal ideation, does the model escalate deterministically? (Forward routing.)

For category-level reasoning we used the base **Llama 2 7B** checkpoint, then drove it with our curated JSON for ten epochs. Held out 20% of categories for evaluation. Fine-tuned weights live behind a self-hosted inference endpoint; the MERN app streams tokens down to the React client via Socket.io.

## The hard lesson

The biggest improvement wasn't from the model. It was from editing the dataset ruthlessly. We deleted ~30% of the responses we'd collected because they drifted toward generic reassurance.

If you're building something similar: **curate like a clinician, not a copywriter**.

Live: **mindmatecare.netlify.app** — the chatbot you talk to is the model I'm describing.

posts.title: Puppeteer Stealth Scraping at Scale: Facebook, Instagram, and Daraz Ad Extraction
posts.subtitle: What we did to keep 50+ Playwright workers alive for hours without getting blocked.
posts.content:
# Puppeteer Stealth Scraping at Scale

**Hunting Goals** scrapes real-time ad signals from Facebook, Instagram, Daraz, OLX, Google Trends, and TikTok — then surfaces the **winning products** Pakistani e-commerce sellers should jump on *before* competitors see them.

Every serious anti-bot on those platforms wants you to fail. Here's what it took to not fail.

## The threat model

- **Facebook & Instagram**: aggressive TLS fingerprinting; `navigator.webdriver`, canvas entropy, audio-context fingerprint, and an in-house bot-ml model
- **Daraz & OLX**: rate-limits by IP, captcha after ~50 requests
- **Google Trends**: nearly impossible at scale — they wrap data in `\u"` JSON escapes and rotate parameterised queries

## Stealth primitives

- **`playwright-extra` + `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth`** to spoof the easy fingerprints
- **Proxy rotation** per worker (residential proxies for FB/IG, datacenter for Trends)
- **Human pacing**: median 1.7 requests/sec per IP, with a long-tail of 0.3–4.0 r/s
- **Randomised canvas events**: scroll, two clicks, occasional key press — anything to perturb session entropy
- **Browser-context isolation**: every worker gets a fresh context, cookies cleared between ad-IDs

## The rate-limit dance

About 1 in 200 worker sessions hits a captcha. We don't solve captchas (we're a legal Pakistani business, so we play by the rules). Instead we **back off and rotate**:

1. Worker sees a CAPTCHA: return 429 to the orchestrator.
2. Orchestrator pulls the session out of the pool for 30 minutes.
3. A fresh proxy + UA fingerprint gets assigned on the next schedule tick.

Across 50 workers this gives a steady-state success rate of about 96%.

## What broke in production

Three things, in order, that I'll never forget:

1. **Facebook silently rolled out new fingerprinting** on a Tuesday morning. We lost 4 hours of data before noticing the empty socket tanks. Recovery: deploy a new UA pool, queue retry of buffered signals, restore from delayed cron.
2. **Google Trends started returning HTML pages** in place of JSON for high-volume IPs. We now proxy all Trends traffic through a dedicated VPN exit-node.
3. **Daraz added Cloudflare Turnstile**. We migrated to a slower but legal poll-based pattern (every 6 minutes), accepting that we lose freshness for that signal.

## Outcome

The system runs **~12,000 ad signals/day** across all sources. The "Win Score" output surfaces ~80 candidate products per day per region, of which ~5 are *actually* worth sellers' attention. Users tell us product-research dropped from 3 hours/week to under 15 minutes.

Live: **huntinggoals.onrender.com**.

posts.title: Building Resilient Async Job Pipelines for the SEO Operator
posts.subtitle: How we run five AI audit agents in parallel without losing a single report to a crashed worker.
posts.content:
# Building Resilient Async Job Pipelines

The **SEO Operator** runs five specialised AI agents (technical audit, keyword research, content review, competitor gap analysis, action-plan synthesis) on the Groq API for every report we generate. The reports frequently take 8–15 minutes.

Doing them synchronously is impossible: the user would time out. Naively queueing them in a single Node process is fragile: any one crashed worker would lose the whole report.

So we built a small state machine. It works.

## Three states, four transitions

Each report is a Mongo document whose `state` field cycles:

`queued → running → done`  
`queued → running → failed`  
`running → failed` (terminal: retry with backoff)
`done` / `failed` (terminal)

Transitions are owned by exactly one component. There is no other writer.

## Why a separate watchdog

The orchestrator dispatches each agent in parallel (`Promise.allSettled` per report). Each agent writes a partial result with `reportId + agentKind` to Mongo as soon as it finishes, so partial loss is bounded — losing one agent means we still keep four.

A second worker — the **cron watchdog** — runs every 5 minutes. It scans for any report that's been `running` for > 20 minutes and:

1. Marks missing agents as `failed`.
2. Re-queues only the failed agents (not the survivors).
3. Emits a `report.partial.completed` event if at least 3 of 5 agents finished.

This makes the system **self-healing** without making it complex.

## What "failed" actually means

It does *not* mean report-died. It means *agent-died-this-time*. The action-plan synthesis agent, on receipt of any partial failures, produces a fuller "known limitations" appendix rather than a synthetic guess. Users see exactly which audits didn't run.

This is honesty I cherish: we never invent data.

## What I'd do differently

We started with **51 automated tests** and now have ~70. The biggest payoff was testing the failure paths, not the happy paths. A report-done-after-cron-restart case caught three critical bugs in the first run.

If you're building any system whose jobs span minutes: **make the watchdog your primary orchestration, not the workers**.

Live: **seo-tracker-drq6.onrender.com** — try a small site first; you'll see all five agents light up.
